headline: Sony completes its purchase of CBS Records
text: Sony closed its $2 billion purchase of CBS Records on 5 January. CBS keeps the right to the CBS name for music recordings, and Sony gets a temporary licence to use it.

headline: Boeing rolls out the 747-400
text: Boeing unveiled its new 747-400 jumbo jet on 26 January. It seats about 416 passengers in three classes, flies up to 7,285 nautical miles and needs only two pilots because of modern cockpit electronics. Northwest Airlines ordered ten of them in October 1985.

headline: Reagan gives his last State of the Union speech
text: President Reagan gave his seventh and final State of the Union address on 25 January. He spoke about the federal deficit, crime, drugs and the line-item veto, and said of welfare: "Some years ago the federal government declared War on Poverty, and poverty won." The race to succeed him is under way.

headline: After the crash, Siemens is worth less than its cash
text: Siemens' stock market value roughly halved during 1987, from 35.2 billion to 18.2 billion marks, and Daimler-Benz fell from 52.2 billion to 26.6 billion. Siemens is now valued about 4 billion marks below the 22 billion marks of cash and liquid assets it reports. In effect, buyers of its shares get the factories and businesses for less than nothing.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 4 January 1988 (review of the German stock market in 1987, citing Commerzbank), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1988-01-04.pdf (read 2026-10-03)

headline: Sam Walton hands the Wal-Mart chief's job to David Glass
text: In February Sam Walton stepped down as chief executive of Wal-Mart, and David Glass took over. Walton stays on as chairman. Wal-Mart is already the most profitable retailer in the United States, though Kmart and Sears still sell more.

headline: Bankgesellschaft's London broker Phillips & Drew is losing money
text: Phillips & Drew, the London broker that Bankgesellschaft fully took over in 1986, is costing its Swiss owner dearly. It lost money on its positions in October's crash, and a rush of orders in the boom before had overwhelmed its system for settling trades. Bankgesellschaft has had to put in fresh money to shore it up.

headline: House votes down Reagan's request for Contra aid
text: On 3 February the House of Representatives rejected President Reagan's request for $36.25 million to aid the Contras, the rebels fighting the government of Nicaragua. It is a setback for his Central America policy.

headline: Calgary Winter Olympics: Dan Jansen falls
text: At the Winter Olympics in Calgary, American speed skater Dan Jansen fell on 14 February after learning that his sister had died. He fell a second time in a later race.

headline: Apple sues Microsoft over Windows
text: Apple sued Microsoft and Hewlett-Packard in March, claiming that Windows 2.0 breaks Apple's copyright by copying elements of the Macintosh screen. The case will test how far a company can protect the look of its software. Windows 2.0 itself has been on sale since December.

headline: Oliver North and John Poindexter indicted in Iran-Contra case
text: A grand jury indicted Marine officer Oliver North and former national security adviser John Poindexter on 16 March. The charges relate to the Iran-Contra affair.

headline: Bush sweeps Super Tuesday as the Democrats split
text: On Super Tuesday, 8 March, George Bush won a majority of the vote in all but three southern states and took 85.7% of the Republican delegates there, putting him far ahead for the nomination. The Democrats split: in the South Jesse Jackson won 286 delegates, Al Gore 259 and Michael Dukakis 193.

headline: Jacobs Suchard raids Rowntree; Nestle offers to help
text: In a dawn raid on 13 April, the Swiss chocolate firm Jacobs Suchard bought 14.9 percent of Britain's Rowntree by 9:15 am. Nestle's managing director Helmut Maucher then called Rowntree chairman Kenneth Dixon and offered to act as a protective buyer. Rowntree makes Kit Kat, After Eight, Smarties and Rolo.

headline: McDonald's signs a deal to open 20 restaurants in Moscow
text: McDonald's Canada signed a joint-venture agreement with Moscow city officials on 29 April to open 20 restaurants in the Soviet capital. Its Canadian boss George Cohon first raised the idea with Soviet sports officials at the 1976 Olympics. It comes as Gorbachev's reforms open the Soviet economy a little.

headline: First flight of the Boeing 747-400
text: The new 747-400 made its first flight on 29 April. It is designed to cut running costs with more efficient engines, winglets on the wing tips and a two-pilot cockpit.

headline: US Navy fights Iran in the Gulf
text: After the frigate USS Samuel B. Roberts struck a mine in the Persian Gulf on 14 April, the US Navy launched Operation Praying Mantis on 18 April against Iranian oil platforms.

headline: Sandoz buys the American anti-corrosion firm Ceilcote
text: Master Builders, Sandoz's building-chemicals company in Cleveland, signed a deal to buy Ceilcote of Berea, Ohio, from General Signal, together with Ceilcote's companies in West Germany, Britain and other countries. Ceilcote protects factory equipment against corrosion. Sandoz keeps growing beyond drugs and dyes.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 30 April 1988 (ap report 'Sandoz übernimmt US-Korrosionsschutzfirma'), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1988-04-30.pdf (read 2026-10-03)

headline: Surgeon General: nicotine is as addictive as heroin
text: On 16 May the US Surgeon General reported that nicotine is as addictive as heroin or cocaine. The finding strengthens the case against cigarettes and is awkward for tobacco makers such as Philip Morris.

headline: Soviet Union begins leaving Afghanistan
text: On 15 May the Soviet army began withdrawing its troops from Afghanistan, after more than eight years of fighting. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev has been restructuring Soviet policy under what he calls perestroika.

headline: Reagan addresses students at Moscow State University
text: On 31 May President Reagan spoke to 600 students at Moscow State University, during his visit to the Soviet capital. The INF treaty that he and Gorbachev signed in December is due to take effect on 1 June.

headline: Nestle wins the battle for Rowntree
text: On 25 June Nestle won the two-month battle for Rowntree with a bid valuing the British chocolate maker at about 2.5 billion pounds, beating Jacobs Suchard. Rowntree is the world's fourth-largest chocolate maker. Nestle sees Rowntree's chocolate bars as a good fit with its own block chocolate.

headline: Who Framed Roger Rabbit opens
text: Disney's Touchstone studio, Steven Spielberg's Amblin and director Robert Zemeckis released Who Framed Roger Rabbit on 22 June, a film mixing live actors and cartoon characters. It cost $50.6 million to make and took $11.2 million on its opening weekend in 1,045 cinemas.

headline: IBM announces the AS/400 for mid-sized businesses
text: IBM announced the AS/400 on 21 June, a family of easy-to-use computers for small and medium-sized companies. IBM and its partners announced more than 1,000 software packages for it at the same time.

headline: INF treaty takes effect
text: The Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty took effect on 1 June. It was signed in December, and the United States and Soviet Union now begin scrapping their medium-range missiles.

headline: GE buys Borg-Warner's plastics business for $2.3 billion
text: General Electric's plastics division bought the chemical business of Borg-Warner, based in Parkersburg, West Virginia, for $2.3 billion in cash: $1 billion from GE's own funds and $1.3 billion borrowed. The unit had $1.25 billion in sales last year and makes ABS plastic for computer cabinets, car parts and football helmets. GE Plastics expects sales of $3 billion this year and $5 billion next year.

headline: US warship shoots down an Iranian airliner, 290 dead
text: The USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655 over the Persian Gulf on 3 July, killing all 290 people aboard. It comes after US Navy clashes with Iranian forces in the Gulf in April.

headline: Piper Alpha oil platform explodes in the North Sea
text: A gas leak and explosion destroyed the Piper Alpha oil platform in the North Sea on 6 July, killing 167 people. The platform was run by Occidental Petroleum.

headline: Democrats nominate Dukakis and Bentsen
text: At their convention the Democrats nominated Michael Dukakis for president and Lloyd Bentsen for vice president on 20 July. They will face Republican George Bush in November.

headline: Iran and Iraq stop fighting
text: A UN-brokered ceasefire between Iran and Iraq began on 20 August. It ends the fighting in the Gulf war.

headline: Pakistan's president Zia dies in a plane crash
text: Pakistan's president Zia-ul-Haq died when his plane crashed on 17 August. The American ambassador, Arnold Raphel, was killed with him.

headline: Night baseball comes to Wrigley Field
text: Chicago's Wrigley Field staged its first night game on 9 August. Until now the park has had no lights.

headline: Another big savings and loan fails
text: American Savings and Loan entered receivership on 5 September, and its assets were bought by the Bass Group. Savings and loan institutions, known as thrifts, are American banks that mostly make home loans.

headline: Bush and Dukakis hold their first debate
text: George Bush and Michael Dukakis met in their first presidential debate on 25 September, at Wake Forest University. Election day is 8 November.

headline: Space shuttle flies again
text: The space shuttle Discovery lifted off on 29 September, the first shuttle flight since the Challenger disaster. It deployed a communications satellite, TDRS-3.

headline: Olympic Games open in Seoul
text: The Summer Olympics opened in Seoul, South Korea, on 17 September. They run until 2 October.

headline: Philip Morris buys Kraft for $13.1 billion
text: Philip Morris and Kraft agreed on 30 October that Philip Morris would buy Kraft at $106 a share, $13.1 billion in total. It began on 17 October with a $90 cash offer, which Kraft rejected. The deal is the second-largest merger in American history and creates the world's largest consumer-goods company, with brands such as Velveeta and Philadelphia cream cheese.

headline: BMW starts building the Z1
text: BMW began production of its Z1 roadster in October at its Munich plant. About 3,500 customers ordered one before production started, and the price is DM 83,000. The car has plastic side panels and doors that slide down into the sills.

headline: Kirk Gibson's home run wins a World Series game
text: Kirk Gibson hit a dramatic home run to win Game 1 of the World Series for the Los Angeles Dodgers on 15 October. The Dodgers went on to beat the Oakland Athletics on 20 October.

headline: Bentsen tells Quayle: 'You're no Jack Kennedy'
text: In the vice-presidential debate in Omaha on 5 October, Senator Lloyd Bentsen told Dan Quayle: 'You're no Jack Kennedy'. The remark stunned Quayle.

headline: Reagan orders the new Moscow embassy torn down
text: President Reagan decided on 27 October to tear down the new American embassy building in Moscow. The reason is Soviet listening devices found in it.

headline: Siemens, Philips and SGS-Thomson join forces on Europe's megachip
text: On 28 October the French-Italian chip maker SGS-Thomson said it will work fully with Siemens and Philips on Jessi, a project to develop a new generation of 'megachips', if the authorities agree. Thomson had pushed for months to join the German and Dutch groups as an equal partner. Europe's chip makers are trying to keep pace with Japan's.
source: Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 1 November 1988 (sda/afp report, Paris, 28 October), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1988-11-01.pdf (read 2026-10-03); Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 30 April 1988 (Japanese memory-chip race), scan data/manual/scans/nzz/NZZ_1988-04-30.pdf (read 2026-10-03)

headline: George Bush wins the US presidency
text: George Bush was elected president on 8 November, defeating Michael Dukakis. He will succeed Ronald Reagan.

headline: KKR bids $25 billion for RJR Nabisco
text: The investment firm KKR agreed on 30 November to buy RJR Nabisco for $25 billion, the largest leveraged buyout so far. In a leveraged buyout the buyers borrow most of the money and repay it from the company's own cash flow.

headline: A self-copying program jams computers across the internet
text: On 2 November a self-copying program, a worm, began to spread across the internet from MIT. It got in through holes in the Unix programs sendmail and finger and also guessed weak passwords, and a flaw made it copy itself onto machines it had already infected, so they slowed to a crawl. About a tenth of the internet was hit, and clearing each machine took about two days of work.

headline: US admits it has a stealth fighter
text: On 10 November the Air Force acknowledged the existence of the F-117 stealth fighter. The Pentagon showed a grainy photograph at a press conference, which ended years of rumours about a secret plane called the F-19.

headline: Nikkei closes above 30,000
text: Tokyo's Nikkei 225 passed 30,000 on 7 December, up from 20,000 less than two years ago, as cheap money keeps pushing up Japanese shares. Banks such as the Industrial Bank of Japan are among the winners.

headline: Pan Am Flight 103 bombed over Lockerbie
text: Pan Am Flight 103 was bombed over Lockerbie, Scotland, on 21 December. The attack killed 270 people.

headline: Swiss minister Elisabeth Kopp resigns over a money-laundering tip-off
text: Swiss Justice Minister Elisabeth Kopp announced on 12 December that she will resign at the end of February, after admitting she had phoned her husband, a board member of Shakarchi Trading, about a money-laundering investigation. Bankgesellschaft, Kreditanstalt and Bankverein held accounts for people in a $1 billion drug-money laundering scheme this year, but deny breaking Swiss law.

headline: Siemens and GEC plan a hostile bid for Plessey
text: On 23 December Siemens of Germany and Britain's GEC, through a joint company called GEC Siemens, made a hostile offer for the British electronics group Plessey, valuing it at 1.7 billion pounds, about $3.1 billion. GEC and Plessey had already merged their phone-equipment businesses in April.

headline: Armenian earthquake kills nearly 25,000
text: An earthquake in Armenia, in the Soviet Union, killed nearly 25,000 people in December. Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev cut short his visit to the United States to return home.

headline: Siemens takes over IBM's loss-making telephone maker Rolm
text: On 13 December IBM agreed to hand Rolm, a leading US maker of business telephone systems, to Siemens; the price was not disclosed. IBM paid 1.26 billion dollars for Rolm in 1984, and it has reportedly lost about 100 million a year since. IBM and Siemens will also form a 50-50 company to sell Rolm products in America, giving Siemens a big foothold there.
